title: Routine childhood vaccination in India from 2005–2006 to 2015–2016: Temporal trends and geographic variation
abstract: OBJECTIVE: India has experienced a substantial increase in the coverage of routine childhood vaccines in recent years. However, a large fraction of these vaccines is not delivered in a timely manner, i.e., at the recommended age. Further, substantial disparities exist in both coverage and timeliness across states. We aim to quantify the changes in coverage and timeliness of routine childhood vaccination in India over time, their variation across states, and changes in these variations over time. METHODS: We used data from two rounds of India's National Family Health Surveys, NFHS-3 (2005-06) and NFHS-4 (2015-16) on bacille Calmette-Guerin vaccine (BCG), three doses of diphtheria, pertussis, and tetanus vaccine (DPT1, DPT2, DPT3), and measles-containing vaccine (MCV). We used the Turnbull estimator to estimate the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of administering each vaccine by a certain age while accounting for two-sided censoring in the survey data. We then used these estimated CDFs to calculate coverage and timeliness at the national and state levels. FINDINGS: At the national level, both vaccination coverage and timeliness estimates increased from NFHS-3 to NFHS-4 for all vaccines. The increase in timeliness ranging from 27.3% for DPT3 to 74.0% for MCV continued to be lower than coverage, ranging from 75.3% (95% CI 57.7-87.2) for DPT3 to 74.0% (95% CI 42.2-33.0) for MCV, for all vaccines. Cross-state variation in timeliness was greater than the variation in coverage. Variation in both timeliness and coverage reduced from NFHS-3 to NFHS-4. However, this reduction was greater for timeliness than for coverage. CONCLUSIONS: A large fraction of the children in India receive vaccines later than the recommended age thereby keeping them exposed to vaccine-preventable diseases. Interventions that specifically focus on improving the timely delivery of vaccines are needed to improve the overall effectiveness of the routine immunization program.

summary.oneLiner: Routine childhood vaccines in India became more widely received between 2005-06 and 2015-16, but many children still get them late, and state gaps are wide.
summary.overview: This paper tracks how many Indian children receive routine vaccines (BCG, three DPT doses and measles-containing vaccine) and how often they get them on schedule. It uses two national family health surveys, from 2005-06 and 2015-16. The authors report that both coverage and timeliness rose over the decade, but a large share of children are still vaccinated later than recommended. They also find that differences between states are larger for timeliness than for coverage, and that these differences narrowed over the period. The authors conclude that programmes focused on on-time delivery are needed.
summary.question: How have the coverage and timeliness of routine childhood vaccination in India changed between 2005-06 and 2015-16, how do these measures vary across states, and how has that variation changed over time?
summary.method: The authors used the Turnbull estimator, a statistical method that estimates the share of children vaccinated by each age even when some children's vaccination dates are incomplete (censored at both ends of the age range). They used these estimates to calculate coverage and timeliness nationally and by state, and compared the two survey rounds.
summary.data: Two rounds of India's National Family Health Surveys: NFHS-3 (2005-06) and NFHS-4 (2015-16). Vaccines covered are BCG, DPT1, DPT2, DPT3 and MCV. The abstract does not state the sample size.
findings: Both vaccination coverage and timeliness rose from NFHS-3 to NFHS-4 for all vaccines at the national level.
Timeliness remained lower than coverage for all vaccines, so a large fraction of children receive vaccines later than the recommended age.
Cross-state variation in timeliness was greater than variation in coverage.
Variation in both timeliness and coverage fell between the two survey rounds, and the fall was greater for timeliness than for coverage.
Caution: the abstract's reported numeric ranges (for example, the confidence interval given for MCV) appear internally inconsistent, so check the full paper before citing specific figures.
The authors conclude that interventions specifically focused on improving timely vaccine delivery are needed to improve the routine immunization program.
summary.whyItMatters: The authors argue that late vaccination leaves children exposed to vaccine-preventable diseases even where coverage is high. They suggest that improving timeliness, not only coverage, is needed to make the national immunization programme more effective. The abstract does not spell out specific actions for managers or policymakers beyond this.
